label: Regular Polygons
notes: This chapter, printed pages twenty-six through thirty-eight, treats a regular polygon as two linked objects at once: a constructible division of a circle into equal arcs, and a finite symmetry machine. We translate straightedge language into roots of unity and symmetry language into matrices and group tables.

label: The Regular n-gon {n}
notes: A regular n-gon has equal sides and equal angles, written with the Schlafli symbol brace n. Its vertices are the n-th roots of unity scaled to the circumcircle, so the figure is exactly one basic rotation applied repeatedly until the orbit closes back on itself.

label: Interior and Exterior Angles
notes: The exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to one full turn, so each exterior angle of a regular n-gon equals two pi over n. The interior angle is its supplement, and the interior angles together total n minus two straight angles exactly, the classical result.

label: Circumradius and Apothem
notes: Drop a perpendicular from the center to a side and you split the central isosceles triangle. The circumradius reaches a vertex while the apothem reaches a side midpoint, related by cosine of pi over n. These two lengths control side length, perimeter, and area together.

label: Roots of Unity
notes: Placing vertices at powers of a primitive n-th root of unity makes the regular polygon an algebraic object. The basic rotation is multiplication by zeta, and every vertex is a power of zeta, which connects polygon geometry directly to cyclotomic field theory and the constructibility question.

label: Star Polygons {n/d}
notes: Keep the same vertices but join each to the one d steps away. When n and d are coprime a single orbit visits all vertices, giving a star polygon brace n over d. The pentagram brace five over two is the smallest genuine example, drawn with one stroke.

label: Density and gcd
notes: The greatest common divisor of n and d decides everything: coprime gives one connected star, while a shared factor splits the drawing into gcd separate compound polygons. The density d counts how many times a central ray crosses edges, which fixes the vertex angle formula.

label: The Dihedral Group D_n
notes: The full symmetry group of a regular n-gon is the dihedral group D n, containing n rotations and n reflections for two n elements total. Rotations alone form the cyclic group C n, and one reflection with the relation s r s equals r inverse generates everything.

label: Two Reflections Make a Rotation
notes: Reflect across one mirror, then a second mirror through the same point, and the composite is a rotation by twice the angle between the mirrors. Reversing the order inverts the rotation, which is the first visibly non-commutative product inside the dihedral group of the polygon.

label: Constructibility (Gauss)
notes: Gauss and Wantzel settled which regular n-gons Euclid's tools can build: exactly those where the odd part of n is a product of distinct Fermat primes. So the seventeen-gon is constructible while the seven and nine-gon are not, a purely arithmetic verdict on geometry.

label: The Trisection Obstruction
notes: Trisecting a sixty degree angle would build two cosine twenty degrees, whose minimal polynomial has degree three. Straightedge and compass only reach numbers through repeated quadratic steps, powers of two, so a degree three irreducible obstruction makes the construction impossible in general for arbitrary angles.

label: Regular Tessellations
notes: Only three regular polygons tile the plane edge to edge: triangles, squares, and hexagons, written brace three six, brace four four, and brace six three. The condition is that the interior angle divides a full turn, which holds solely for these three orders.

label: Recap and Takeaways
notes: Regular polygons are circle orbits filtered by arithmetic for construction and organized by dihedral symmetry for motion. Roots of unity unify both views, star polygons reuse the same vertices with a longer step, and only three regular tilings survive the angle-sum constraint of the plane.
